title: Make me an instrument
hookLine: the prayer called Francis's comes from long after him, but carries his spirit

lines: A PRAYER WITH HIS NAME ON IT.
cards: There's a prayer that turns up on cards, on kitchen walls, on the backs of service sheets, sometimes printed with a name underneath: Saint Francis. It begins by asking to be made an instrument of peace.
Here's the surprise. It isn't found in anything from Francis's own time. Those who've traced it find it long after him, in French, in a small church publication, with no author's name at all.
Somewhere along the way it picked up his name and kept it. So why does it carry his name so easily? Some readers say it's because it sounds like him.

teach.h: HATRED FOR LOVE, DOUBT FOR FAITH.
teach.b: The prayer is built in two halves. The first is a list of swaps. Where there's hatred, it asks to bring love.
Where there's injury, pardon. Then doubt and faith, despair and hope, darkness and light, sadness and joy. Each line asks to carry into a room the opposite of what's already in it.

teach.h: TO CONSOLE, NOT TO BE CONSOLED.
teach.b: The second half turns the usual wish around: not so much to be consoled as to console, to be understood as to understand, to be loved as to love.
It ends with reversals that sound like the Gospel: it is in giving that we receive, in pardoning that we are pardoned, in dying that we are born to eternal life. Now the word instrument.

Paul uses it in his letter to the Romans: "yield yourselves unto God, as those that are alive from the dead, and your members as instruments of righteousness unto God." An instrument doesn't play itself.
A violin doesn't pick the tune; it only has to be in tune, and in the right hands. That's the humility here. The prayer doesn't promise to make peace by sheer effort.
It asks to be used. And Jesus blessed exactly that work: "Blessed are the peacemakers: for they shall be called the children of God." So does it matter that Francis didn't write it?
Set it beside this week: the clothes handed back, the cold gate borne patiently, the wolf called brother. Written far from Assisi, long after him, it still lets some readers hear his voice.
A prayer can carry a saint's spirit without carrying his signature.

how: Christians in a range of churches pray the Peace Prayer, known as the Prayer of Saint Francis, alone or together, and it is also sung as a hymn.

games.q: what does “make me an instrument” mean?
o: asking God to use you as a tool for peace
a vow to play music in church for God
asking God to make you strong enough to win

games.q: the peace prayer — tap the pairs.

s: Francis wrote the peace prayer himself
it isn't in anything from his own time; it turns up long after him, in French, unsigned.
Paul writes of yielding your members as instruments of righteousness
in his letter to the Romans: instruments of righteousness unto God.
the prayer's second half asks above all to be understood and loved
it turns that around: to understand rather than be understood, to love rather than be loved.

games.q: a friend shows you a card: the Prayer of Saint Francis. who wrote it?
o: Francis himself, in his own lifetime.
an unnamed writer, in French, long after him.
Brother Leo, writing down what Francis said.
games.why: it appears long after Francis, in French, with no author's name. it carries his spirit, not his signature.

practice: If you know the prayer and you pray, say it once, slowly, letting each pair land before the next; if you pray but don't know it, take Jesus's line instead: blessed are the peacemakers.
If you don't pray, choose one pair from the list, hatred and love, despair and hope, and sit with one place in your life where that swap is needed.

wordCard.voice: Make me an instrument. The opening request of the peace prayer that carries Francis's name: not to do great things, but to be used for peace.

orig.note: Greek in Romans 6:13 for instruments: tools, or weapons, put to a purpose.

carryVoice: Your line: an instrument of peace. A violin only has to be in tune. Same time tomorrow.
